title: The Patient Prathap Reddy Could Not Send Abroad
dek: After a 38-year-old patient died in 1979 for want of $50,000, a Madras cardiologist spent four years pushing a corporate hospital through land rules, loans and customs.

story.event: Deciding to build a corporate hospital in Madras after a patient died unable to afford surgery abroad, and the four years of permissions that followed
story.summary: In December 1979 the Madras cardiologist Prathap C. Reddy lost a 38-year-old patient who could not raise $50,000 for bypass surgery in the United States, and resolved to build a hospital offering such care in India. Working through land-ceiling rules, a lack of bank finance for hospitals and heavy duties on equipment, he secured help from Indira Gandhi and Pranab Mukherjee and a public share issue, and the 150-bed Apollo Hospital in Madras was inaugurated on 18 September 1983.
paragraphs: In December 1979 Prathap Reddy, a cardiologist in Madras, lost a patient he had been trying to send abroad. The man, 38, should have had bypass surgery in the United States that October with the surgeon Denton Cooley, but could not raise $50,000. Reddy later described the man's 31-year-old widow sitting beside him with their two small children. "Why can't we do this here?" he remembered asking himself.

He had come home from the United States in the early 1970s after a letter from his father, and had built a busy practice in a small private nursing home. Bypass surgery was available at only one or two Indian institutions, with results he considered unacceptable. The obstacles to doing better were plain. Hospitals could not get bank loans, and imported equipment was taxed as a luxury. By one doctor's account, only government or charitable hospitals could then exceed 30 beds. Colleagues told him to buy the plot next door and add 50 beds instead.

He chose the larger plan: a full hospital, run as a company and named Apollo. By his account the land alone took 18 months to two years because of land-ceiling rules. Week after week he flew to Delhi on Thursday evening and came back on Sunday morning, meeting officials, and importing equipment meant a dozen separate applications. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, keen to reverse India's brain drain, had the customs duty waived on condition that Apollo treated some patients free, he said, and the finance minister, Pranab Mukherjee, let it borrow as a special case. Bombay bankers called listing a hospital crazy until one came to see the place after Reddy's evening clinic and underwrote a share issue, subscribed in December 1982.

President Zail Singh inaugurated the 150-bed hospital on Greams Road on 18 September 1983; it began admitting patients the following February. Apollo became India's largest hospital chain. The historian Sarah Hodges has argued that admiring retellings of its founding overstate how much Apollo changed Indian healthcare and how far one man changed government policy, and in 2004 Der Tagesspiegel noted that its care was beyond the reach of India's estimated 300 million poor. "I was not then, and even now I'm not an entrepreneur," Reddy said in 2024.

quote.text: When the multitude hate a man, it is necessary to examine into the case. When the multitude like a man, it is necessary to examine into the case.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Confucius asks for the same scrutiny of someone the crowd admires as of someone it condemns. Reddy's account of grief turned into a hospital is moving and largely documented; a historian finds the wider legend inflated. The line asks us to hold both, this retelling included.

reflection: Reddy's grief was real, and so were the Thursday flights and the dozen applications. The legend that grew around them is a different thing: tidier, and kinder to its hero. Every organisation that lasts acquires a story like that, and the people inside it often come to believe the tidy version.

You are living through the untidy version now, with its delays, its help from people who will never be named, and decisions that were less certain than they will later look. It is worth keeping an honest record of it for your own sake. On a hard day the true account is often more encouraging than the legend, because it shows how ordinary the steps were.
invitation: Write a short, plain note about one week in your work that a later story might tidy up, and include the name of someone who helped and will probably never be credited.

sources.title: Dr. Prathap C. Reddy: interview by Tarun Khanna, Mumbai, 29 April 2014 (Creating Emerging Markets oral history)
sources.publisher: Baker Library Special Collections, Harvard Business School
sources.supports: Reddy's own account (summary on this page; full transcript PDF linked from it): his father's letter and return to India; practice in a small private nursing home; bypass surgery available at one or two Indian institutions with unacceptable results; referring patients to Denton Cooley; the young man lost in December 1979 who should have had surgery in October but could not raise $50,000, his 31-year-old wife and two children; 'Why can't we do this here?'; advice to add 50 beds next door instead; the Land Ceiling Act (two years, or almost 18 months, for land clearance); hospitals not eligible for funding; equipment charged as a luxury item; Indira Gandhi's interest in reversing the brain drain and the customs duty exemption on condition that some patients were treated free; Pranab Mukherjee allowing Apollo, as a special case, to borrow half from banks and half as a foreign-exchange loan; weekly trips to Delhi from Thursday evening to Sunday morning; 12 applications for 360 kinds of equipment; investment bankers calling a hospital listing crazy and one underwriting the issue after an evening visit; the issue in December 1982; inauguration by the President on 18 September 1983.

sources.title: Apollo's Healthcare Architect (7 October 2024)
sources.supports: Return from the US after his father's letter; the 38-year-old with two young children lost in 1979 because he could not raise $50,000; land restricted by the Land Ceiling Act; hospitals not eligible for bank funding; customs duty on equipment given as 300%; Pranab Mukherjee clearing funding from six banks; inauguration in September 1983 by President Giani Zail Singh on Greams Road; nearly 60 trips to Delhi; Reddy aged 50 at the first hospital; 'I was not then, and even now I'm not an entrepreneur'; his four daughters running the group.

sources.title: Doctor, Father, Entrepreneur: Here's what makes Apollo Hospitals founder Dr. Prathap C. Reddy one of India's best-known business tycoons (12 March 2024)
sources.supports: Reddy in his own words: the birthday letter from his father; referring patients to friends in the US and to Denton Cooley; the 38-year-old patient in 1979 who could not afford to travel and died; hospitals unable to secure bank loans and not recognised as an industry; equipment treated as a luxury at 100% duty; meeting Indira Gandhi; the 1983 inauguration by Zail Singh.

sources.title: "It all changed after Apollo": healthcare myths and their making in contemporary India (Sarah Hodges, Indian Journal of Medical Ethics, vol. 10, no. 4, October-December 2013)
sources.supports: Historian's critical account (full text in the PDF linked from the page): land on Greams Road announced in 1980; a Chennai doctor's statement that only government or charitable trust hospitals could previously exceed 30 beds; overseas borrowing and the first public share issue for such a hospital; inauguration in September 1983 by Zail Singh and admission of patients only from February 1984; the argument that claims that Apollo changed everything and that Reddy single-handedly changed government policy are myths, and that Apollo's main success has been image management.

sources.title: Eine Herzoperation für 4000 Dollar (3 May 2004)
sources.supports: Independent account of the 1979 patient, a young businessman needing a bypass whom Reddy advised to fly to the US, who could not afford it and died; restrictions on bank credit, land and equipment imports; the first hospital opened in Madras in 1983; Apollo's treatment unaffordable for an estimated 300 million poor Indians.

sources.title: Apollo Hospitals' Prathap Reddy grooms daughters for leadership positions (24 November 2014)
sources.supports: The first Apollo was a 150-bed hospital in Chennai in 1983; the daughters' early involvement.

sources.title: Apollo Hospitals (interview introduction)
sources.supports: Apollo incorporated as a public limited company in 1979, promoted by Prathap C. Reddy; growth from a 150-bed hospital in Chennai.

cross_checks.claim: In 1979 Reddy lost a 38-year-old patient who could not raise the money for heart surgery in the United States
Hospitals could not get bank finance and medical equipment was taxed as a luxury
Finance minister Pranab Mukherjee cleared bank funding for Apollo as a special case
Apollo raised money through a public share issue
The 150-bed hospital in Madras was inaugurated by President Zail Singh in September 1983

research_notes: The patient: Reddy's 2014 HBS oral history is the fullest account (December 1979; surgery due in October with Denton Cooley; $50,000; widow aged 31, children aged four and two); Fortune India (2024) agrees on 38, two young children and $50,000; Business Today (2024, Reddy's own words) gives 1979 and 38 but no sum; Der Tagesspiegel (2004) calls him a young businessman needing a bypass and gives no sum. The story uses the oral history, attributed. The transcript names Cooley; Fortune India, Business Today and Der Tagesspiegel say the US; the story does not name a city. Customs duty: Reddy gave 375% in 2014, Fortune India reports 300% in 2024, and Reddy told Business Today 100% in 2024; the story says only that equipment was taxed as a luxury. Land: the transcript says both 'two years' and 'almost 18 months'; the story gives both. Delhi trips: 'every Thursday ... week after week' (oral history) versus 'almost 60 trips' (Fortune India); the story uses Reddy's description. Bank finance: the HBS summary says Mukherjee's 1982 mandate let Apollo borrow half from a state bank and half as a foreign-exchange loan, with the money arriving in 1983; Fortune India quotes Reddy that six banks would lend Rs 5 crore each; the story says only that Mukherjee let it borrow as a special case. Share issue: the transcript dates the subscribed issue to December 1982; Hodges confirms it was the first public offering to finance such a hospital; IUP says Apollo was incorporated as a public limited company in 1979. The account of Indira Gandhi's duty waiver, conditional on free treatment for some patients, is Reddy's own and attributed. The 30-bed limit is a Chennai doctor's statement quoted by Hodges and is attributed as one doctor's account. Hodges (2013) is included because she argues that the standard Apollo story overstates Reddy's role and Apollo's effect; the story reports her view in her name, and that Apollo opened in September 1983 but admitted patients only from February 1984. The HBS transcript PDF is linked from the Baker Library page through an expiring signed URL, so the stable landing page is cited. Global Indian (2025) repeats the Thursday-to-Sunday quotation but is not cited. The Confucius saying is applied by analogy to the founding story's reception.
